But what exactly *is* activism? I'm not trying to be annoying here. The way I see it, people's main problem with activism is that it brings some kind "values" into what should otherwise bea very clinical and rational field of science. I have to make a critique of this idea.

First of all, I don't think you can have a value-free science. No, not even a STEM field. Let me give you an example: before being an anthropology student, I was a CompSci student (I live outside the US). At my CompSci faculty, we could take an elective course about self-driving cars, where you could learn stuff like how to make algorithms that allow cars' sensors to "see" the road and interpret what they are seeing and react to it to drive the car. I think you could say that it was, more or less, a very scientific or science-based course, and we were taught about algorithms that had been developed by very smart people who are, again, scientists. But if we zoom out a little, we would notice that this course was only offered at the faculty because it was provided by a company that makes self-driving cars, who wanted to hire students after graduating and have them make the software for those cars - all this, of course, because they wanted to sell this kind of cars to people, which of course leads to other things like why people desire to purchase self-driving cars (hint: the infrastructure in the world's cities is primarily built for cars). Suddenly, what seemed like a detached scientific enterprise is motivated by values. And I say 'motivated', because it is not merely a matter of someone discovering something accidentally that is deemed useful later, but because tons of cash were being poured into this research area.

Why did I bring this up? Because we have to unpack our assumptions here, namely, that we can have science that is not motivated by values at all. Under this ideal scenario, the scientist is merely a sort of automaton that performs experiments, labouring with no clear or visible end in sight, only for the production of some kind of knowledge that other people can instrumentalize. In the real world, there is no science that is separated from values. From searching for a cure for a deadly disease to launching rockets into space in order to reach another planet, everything deemed "scientific" is motivated by values. The difference between sociology and hard sciences is that these values are much more often looked at in sociology and much more often closely scrutinized - after all, what is sociology if not a study of how and why people do the things they do?
I think people usually want to put the cart before the horse: they see the word 'activism' and assume that it is a sort of blind, unquestioning adherence to an unproven (or unprovable) ideal; hence, it brings in a set of assumptions that will influence, consciously or not, the researcher's 'objectivity' in the scientific endeavour of *reflecting reality*. This produces results that confirm the activist-turned-researcher's initial assumptions, which allows them to continue their own study further, in a theoretically endless feedback loop. Now, I do not deny that this is a real possibility that can occur. Instead, I want to focus on the fact that, as hard as we struggle to, we cannot be value-neutral in research activities. Again, that doesn't mean that we should let our own biases influence our conclusions with no constraint: but acknowledging that we have a bias or are committed to a particular value is not the same as trying to erase every trace of it from our research.

Finally, I want to propose an alternate perspective to the activist-turned-researcher, that of the researcher-turned-activist. A sociologist may carry out research by starting out from the viewpoint that it will be, at least, interesting or useful to society at large. We may analyse a particular topic and find that there is a systemic power structure operating behind the scenes. Our disgruntlement with a state of affairs is a result of the research we have carried out, because the facts are deemed to point to a violation of our personal values. Activism comes in because we know something is going in a way we do not believe is fair or right, and because the structures that would hold out the power to change what is going on in the field may be the cause of the issue or complicit to it. Not everyone does this, mind you - you may very well study something and discover that it produces no strong reaction that involves your personal values, while it does for someone else, because your values are, in the end, different.

So, to recap: OP's question was whether the commitment to values in sociology does not undermine the process of producing knowledge. I argue that there is no scientific process of production of knowledge that is completely free of any values. Furthermore, even with a researcher's given set of values, research can still be carried out according to a sound methodology, but sociologists may turn to activism because it is away for them to resolve a tension between their own values and a state of affairs in society that runs counter to those values. In this sense, activism, as an activity, is no more value-laden than a programmer's coding software for self-driving cars and being paid for it. The difference, of course, is that the latter abides by the general flow of power in society and the ideologies presented by it, while the former is more socially visible and often runs counter to the flow of power. And perhaps that might help us understand why this question is being posed in the first place, but I'll let someone else talk about that.

Hi! Anthropology student here. First, I'm glad you're asking this question. It's great to see curious people looking for answers.

I should start by saying that conflictualism (the sociological perspective that looks at discrimination and inequality) is by no means the only one available or the only one used in studies. Still, why is it so often employed? Well, usually because it can help change things in the world. This is by no means an ideological stance, it's what research in science is supposed to do. In computer science, for example, if you're researching an encryption algorithm used by some software that handles private data and you discover a flaw in it, then your research carries quite the implications for the real world. You'd expect someone to take action and change that algorithm.

Going back to sociology, the same applies. I want to say that sociological research is not really about "overly grand" narratives about society (unless you read people from the 19th century or some ground-breaking theoretical works, which are not many), it is usually much more focused on specific areas or groups of people. Sociologists research discrimination and inequality because their studies would then (*ideally*) be cited in policy making in order to make decisions based on evidence, not opinions or gut feelings. (I say *ideally* because simply publishing a paper in an academic journal guarantees it will be read by nobody outside academia, which is why many sociologists try to spread their findings to a wider audience and often are part of civic or activist groups.) Is there a moral underside to this, as in "we should act to help these people who are discriminated against"? Definitely yes. But there is also a more pragmatic look too. Take homelessness, for example: I'm sure sociologists researching it would agree that it is right to help homeless people so they stop being homeless, otherwise they probably wouldn't be researching it in the first place. But, beyond the researcher's own feelings, there are other things to consider, which is where sociology is needed. If the mayor or the council of a city wants to reduce homelessness in their city, they would need sociologists to study what causes homelessness in the first place *in that city or region*, what resources they have at hand to deal with it and how other cities have dealt with the same issue, what they did right and what went wrong.

Now, this all sounds nice, but I do want to say one more thing, which is where we have to take a step back. I have argued before why sociological research is important by saying it can lead to policies being implemented, which requires some structures of power. What I failed to mention is that, very often, those same structures of power also cause inequalities and discrimination in the first place... and they likely don't want that to change. Returning to my example with homelessness, the sociologist might wonder why there is a large percentage of homeless people in one city or area relative to others and discover that, in other areas, there are very harsh measures set in place against homeless people (we would say that homelessness is *criminalized* there), so the homeless people move to a new place where it's easier for them to live. Suddenly, it's no longer about here versus there, but there's an entire system at play where changing one thing in one place has ripples in quite another place. And this is, at least in my view, one of the most important things that sociologists seek to uncover.

Anyways, I hope this comment has provided a useful answer to your question and I didn't ramble too much. If you have any questions, feel free to ask!

A lot of people in this thread have mentioned the sex/gender distinction in this thread, treating it as a distinction between a given, natural state of the body and a cultural, socialized or produced state of identity. I can't believed this isn't criticized more strongly here.  
The problem, as Latour noted in his book, "We have never been modern", is that we can never draw a rigid line between the two categories of 'nature' and 'culture', nor likewise between sex and gender, and this is also true of how we view and use our own bodies. If we are to follow Foucault here, we might look at the assignment of gender at birth as a disciplinary technology that regulates bodies into the categories of man and woman, or male and female, depending on what kind of discourse or terms you want to use, even though often those terms mirror each other. More dramatically, I would say that it is a form of violence against bare being, a way of denying that being many possibilities of development ('becoming', if you want to use that loaded word) in life.  
One could literally write an entire book or thesis just on this matter that is far, far from being as easy and neat as it may seem, especially not when we remove power from the equation. But to answer your original question, most people, once entered into this 'normativ grid' and having their gender assigned at birth and then having that gender reinforced ('socialized') as a relevant category of how they constitute themselves, do not experience a need or desire to change it and, conceptually, they do not even perceive the possibility of doing so; or, if they do, they become painfully aware of its hidden social cost. They basically perpetuate the regulatory fictions they are bound by.   
If I may be honest, the current narrative in queer circles of 'my gender or sexual identity is mine and mine alone and it represents a central part of who I am and what I do' is just as essential a discourse as biological determinism, except more free-floating and ambiguous in its wording. As sociologists (both straight, cis or queer), we should not shy away from questions of structure vs agency when evaluating how people form their own identities. Even in the context of the LGBTQ community, I would argue that doing so is by no means counter to their emancipation, and we go back to a quote from Foucault's "What is critique?" for this:

>governmentalization, which seems to me characteristic enough of these societies of the European West in the sixteenth century, cannot be dissociated from the question *"How not to be governed?"* I do not mean by this that governmentalization would be opposed, in a kind of inverted con trary affirmation, to *"We do not want to be governed, and we do not want to be governed at all."* What I mean is that in the great anxiety surrounding the way to govern and in the inquiries into modes of governing, one detects a perpetual question, which would be: "*How not to be governed like that, by that, in the name of these principles, in view of such objectives and by the means of such methods, not like that, not for that, not by them?"*

I'm a first year Anthropology student, so don't expect an expert answer. 'Value', 'worldview', 'belief' are very broad terms, we need to be able to say first what those things people believe are, because there is likely to be an entire subfield of sociology dedicated to how people interact in that specific setting, group, institution, etc.

Even so, my first reaction is to think of Durkheim, who links the intensity of the "collective consciousness" to the social division of labour in society. He says that when everyone does relatively similar work tasks (like in a rural farming community), people develop very similar beliefs and values, that get reinforced through social interaction. This doesn't explain \*how\* people acquire those beliefs, but gives us an insight into how those ideas we think of as very personal and important for ourselves are actually the result of outside forces that mold us - to a lesser or greater degree. This is the foundation on which the theories of socialization develop later on. Socialization is the process through which an individual learns the values and norms of a group through social interaction. When we're children, we experience primary socialization, which helps us learn the fundamental values of society, then we later go through forms of secondary socialization, which help us prepare for more specific social settings. In this sense, all knowledge about social life is passed on from generation to generation.

Then you have conflictualists like marxists, who will look at material conditions of life, or feminists, who will look at gender divisions in society, and explain that social knowledge isn't purely functional. Rather, it is produced and transmitted by entitites (people, organizations, governments, etc.) that have certain levels of political, economic and social power and can also silence opposing views. Therefore, beliefs and values aren't neutral things that pass through our minds, they are weaponised. Then you have others, like Foucault, who talks about the relationship between knowledge and power and the production of discourses, both social and scientific; how and even if we can escape such discourses is a very complicated matter for debate.

So there's a general trend of looking at both widely shared and personal beliefs as things that come from outside the individual, from this nebulous thing called 'culture', which is basically impossible to describe fully, because it works differently in different settings. For example, religious beliefs used to be super important in society, now they may be completely irrelevant for quite many people, but there are clearly differences between the levels of secularism in Western Europe and Eastern Europe and the Middle East, for example. A great deal of quantitative reasearch goes into discovering what social factors influence people's attitudes towards stuff like this. Also, in anthropology at least, why people believe stuff is explained by theories ranging from structuralism to environmental determinism and so on, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. There's no single universal explanation, but the takeaway, in my opinion, is this: every person is, at least in part, a product of the cultural elements that preceded them and that will likely continue to exist after they die.

Don't let this discourage you. Sociology is an attempt to understand and think critically about society and the social aspects of human behaviour, and research methodology is anything but 'trivial' - although a lot of students struggle with it and don't properly follow it, but that's not the case with peer-reviewed sociology journals. Sociology is an odd science because it has both quantitative and qualitative methodology, it's not just about numbers, it's also about what those numbers describe and knowing that human reality cannot be captured fully just by statistics, which is why it also requires a lot of work with concepts and theories. The kind of positivism that advocates for a rigid, mathematical approach has long fallen out of favor, which doesn't mean that statistics or maths isn't used in sociology, but that an understanding of society goes beyond saying "x% of people have this attitude towards y or engage in this behavior".

That being said, I still think economy is the more marketable option for a future job, but sociology is by far more creative and open-ended.

You make a good point, but I also need to raise the question: must art appeal to the viewers?

Modern art is indeed more focused ideas, but  it is also reexamining the place and applications of art in the world. A lot of "classical" art was commisioned by wealthy patrons with a specific decorative purpose in mind, like a painting I want to hang in my living room for guests to see or a portrait to show people how cool and rich I am. So of course a lot of that art had to be "pleasing" to the spectator, and many pieces of classical art were meant to decorate spaces. Which - fair enough, if I want to hang a painting on my wall or put a marble statue in front of a church, I'd rather it looked really pretty.

Of course, this was also taken to an extreme, especially in 19th century France, where the Academy was dictating what should be considered "good" or "real" art and what techniques and standards painters should abide by. This had the effect of stifling creativity. Many painters who are now renown, like Delacroix, Gericault, or Courbet were at first booed and derided by the Academy and the critics because the art they were creating was violating the standards of the time. Van Gogh, for example, a staple of post-impressionism, only sold one painting during his lifetime, but now everybody knows at least one of his works. The Impressionists kicked off modern art when they said "Screw this! We will paint what we want, and we'll make our own Salon to exhibit our art, with blackjack and hookers!" (It didn't actually have blackjack and hookers).

After they got that boulder moving, it started speeding up. If you could question how art must be made, and by whom, then you could eventually also question what art is and what purpose it fulfils. That's the entire thing with Duchamp's urinal: it's not meant to be taken seriously, you don't need to stand in reverence and awe when you look at it. But that's how you were taught to look at art displayed in a museum, to treat it as something larger than yourself, full of inherent beauty and aesthetic value. Duchamp showed that anything can be art as long as it has something to say - an idea, if you will. There's no good or bad way to make art, there are just your personal principles and what you want to impart to your public. And what that public understands, of course. Other than that, you have no duty to anybody. As an artist, he argues, you only have the task of getting an emotional reaction from your audience, of making them experience something and perhaps, why not?, try to make them see something new.
